title: Integration on ℕ is summation
promptMarkdown:
Let $X=\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ with $\mathcal M=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)$ and $\mu$ the counting measure.

1. Prove, from the definition of the integral as a supremum over simple functions, that for every $f:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty]$
$$\int_{\mathbb N}f\,d\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f(k).$$
Handle the case in which $f(k)=\infty$ for some $k$ separately.
2. Deduce from Theorem 0.3 of lecture 4, in a few lines, that for any doubly indexed family $a_{ij}\ge0$ ($i,j\in\mathbb N$) one has $\sum_i\sum_ja_{ij}=\sum_j\sum_ia_{ij}$.
3. Give an explicit sequence of functions $f_n\ge0$ on $\mathbb N$ with $f_n\to0$ pointwise and $\int f_n\,d\mu=1$ for every $n$. Which hypothesis of the monotone convergence theorem fails for your sequence, and what does Fatou's lemma assert about it (is the inequality strict)?
hintLadder: Truncate: when $f$ is finite-valued, $s_N=f\chi_{\{1,\dots,N\}}$ is a simple function below $f$. Compute $\int s_N\,d\mu$.
For the reverse inequality take an arbitrary measurable simple $0\le s\le f$ and compare $\int s\,d\mu$ with $\sum_k s(k)$; watch for a value $\alpha_i>0$ carried on an infinite set.
View the double family as a sequence of functions $f_j(i)=a_{ij}$ on $\mathbb N$ and apply Theorem 0.3 of lecture 4 together with part 1.
A moving bump: a function equal to $1$ at a single point that drifts to infinity.

deterministicChecks.description: checking the identity for particular finite ranges is not a proof for all f

criteria.criterion: ∫ f ≥ Σ f(k) via the truncations f·χ_{1..N} (simple, below f, with integral the partial sum), plus the separate argument when some f(k) = ∞ (both sides infinite, using s = m·χ_{k}).

levels.label: met
levels.description: Truncation argument and the infinite-value case.

criteria.criterion: ∫ f ≤ Σ f(k): for an arbitrary simple 0 ≤ s ≤ f, either some positive value is carried on an infinite set (then Σ f(k) = ∞) or ∫ s = Σ_k s(k) ≤ Σ_k f(k).
The double-series identity deduced by reading Σ_j ∫ f_j = ∫ Σ_j f_j through part 1.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Theorem cited without the translation to sums.

criteria.criterion: A correct sequence (e.g. χ_{n}) with pointwise limit 0 and integrals 1; monotonicity identified as the failing hypothesis; Fatou's inequality 0 ≤ 1 stated and recognised as strict.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Example right, hypothesis or Fatou discussion missing.

checkExamples.label: general argument
checkExamples.text: Let f be finite-valued and for every N put s_N = f·χ_{1..N}, a simple function with s_N ≤ f and ∫ s_N = Σ_{k≤N} f(k). Taking the supremum over N gives ∫ f ≥ Σ_k f(k). Conversely for an arbitrary simple s ≤ f, ∫ s = Σ_k s(k) ≤ Σ_k f(k) unless some positive value sits on an infinite set, in which case both sides are infinite.

checkExamples.label: instances only
checkExamples.text: For n=1 the integral of f·χ_{1} is f(1), for n=2 it is f(1)+f(2), for n=3 it is f(1)+f(2)+f(3), so the integral equals the sum.
